book: The Kalama Sutta — The Charter of Free Inquiry

1: The Kalamas of Kesamutta said to the Buddha: Lord, there are some ascetics and brahmins who come to Kesamutta. They explain and glorify their own doctrines, but they dispraise, revile, and disparage the doctrines of others. And then other ascetics come, and they too glorify their own doctrine and disparage the rest. We are doubtful and uncertain, Lord: which of these venerable ascetics speaks the truth, and which speaks falsehood?
[Kalama Sutta — Do not go by report]

It is proper for you, Kalamas, to be doubtful, for you are uncertain; for among you has arisen a perplexity. Come, Kalamas — do not go by report, by tradition, by hearsay, by what is in the scriptures, by logical conjecture, by inference, by consideration of appearances, by a pleasing theory, or by the thought 'this ascetic is our teacher.'

But when you know for yourselves: these things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, if undertaken and practised, lead to harm and to suffering — then, Kalamas, abandon them.
2: What do you think, Kalamas: when greed arises in a man, does it arise for his benefit or for his harm? For his harm, Lord. A greedy man, overcome by greed, kills a living being, takes what is not given, goes with the wife of another, speaks falsehood, and leads others into such conduct too — for a long time this brings him harm and suffering.

When a noble disciple is thus freed from greed, from ill-will, from confusion, and is watchful and aware, he dwells with a heart filled with loving-kindness, with compassion, with sympathetic joy, with equanimity, extending over all the world. And he finds joy in four things: If there is a next world, I shall be reborn in a happy state. If there is no next world, still in this life I live free of hatred and ill-will. If evil comes to evildoers, then no evil will come to me, for I do no evil. If evil does not come to evildoers, then I am doubly pure.

The Kalamas said: Wonderful, Lord! Wonderful! We go to the Buddha for refuge, to the dharma, and to the sangha. And the Buddha said: Whatever among these things you have tested for yourselves and found wholesome, that undertake and abide in — for your own good, and for the good of others.
